Unit 6 Seminar: K-Means Clustering Tutorial¶

Module: Machine Learning (PCOM7E), University of Essex Online

Datasets: iris.csv and wine.csv (UCI Machine Learning Repository) and weatherAUS.csv (Kaggle), all supplied with the seminar brief and stored under 05-machine-learning/datasets/.

The brief asks for at least one of three tasks. All three are carried out here, because Task C differs in kind from the other two: A and B have known labels to compare against, whereas C has none and asks instead for a sweep of K with visualisation. Doing all three makes the comparison between the labelled and unlabelled cases possible, which is where the useful conclusion sits.

Dependencies¶

pandas, numpy, scikit-learn and matplotlib.

In [1]:
import pandas as pdlib
import numpy as nplib
import matplotlib.pyplot as pltlib
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score, silhouette_score

datasetRoot = "../../datasets"
randomSeed = 42

A note on method, applying to all three tasks¶

K-means assigns points to the nearest centroid by Euclidean distance, and that has two consequences that shape everything below.

Non-numeric columns must go. Euclidean distance is undefined over species names or yes/no strings. The label columns are therefore removed before clustering and held back purely for comparison afterwards, which is what the brief means by removing a few columns.

Scale is not neutral. An attribute measured in hundreds contributes far more to the distance than one measured in fractions, regardless of which carries more information. Standardising to zero mean and unit variance removes that arbitrariness. Whether it helps is an empirical question, and Tasks A and B answer it in opposite directions, so both are run each way rather than assuming the answer.

In [2]:
def summariseAgreement(trueLabels, clusterLabels):
    crossTab = pdlib.crosstab(trueLabels, clusterLabels)
    bestMatchTotal = crossTab.max(axis=1).sum()
    return crossTab, bestMatchTotal, bestMatchTotal / len(trueLabels)


def fitClustering(featureMatrix, clusterCount):
    model = KMeans(n_clusters=clusterCount, n_init=10, random_state=randomSeed)
    return model.fit(featureMatrix)

Task A: Iris data¶

Perform K-means on iris.csv with K = 3 and compare the clusters against the three species labels.

In [3]:
irisFrame = pdlib.read_csv(f"{datasetRoot}/iris/iris.csv")

print("Shape:", irisFrame.shape)
print("*" * 58)
print(irisFrame.head().to_string(index=False))
print("*" * 58)
print("Species counts:")
print(irisFrame["species"].value_counts().to_string())
print("Missing values:", int(irisFrame.isna().sum().sum()))

The four measurements are all in centimetres and span a similar range, so this dataset is already close to commensurate. The species column is the label and is removed before clustering.

In [4]:
irisFeatures = irisFrame.drop(columns=["species"])
irisTruth = irisFrame["species"]
irisScaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(irisFeatures)

for variantName, variantData in [("Unscaled", irisFeatures.values), ("Standardised", irisScaled)]:
    fitted = fitClustering(variantData, 3)
    crossTab, matched, agreement = summariseAgreement(irisTruth, fitted.labels_)
    print(f"{variantName} (K = 3)")
    print("*" * 58)
    print(crossTab.to_string())
    print(f"  adjusted Rand index      = {adjusted_rand_score(irisTruth, fitted.labels_):.4f}")
    print(f"  best-match agreement     = {matched}/{len(irisTruth)} = {agreement:.4f}")
    print()

Unscaled (K = 3)
**********************************************************
col_0        0   1   2
species               
setosa       0  50   0
versicolor  48   0   2
virginica   14   0  36
  adjusted Rand index      = 0.7302
  best-match agreement     = 134/150 = 0.8933

Standardised (K = 3)
**********************************************************
col_0        0   1   2
species               
setosa       0  50   0
versicolor  39   0  11
virginica   14   0  36

  best-match agreement     = 125/150 = 0.8333

Task A results¶

On the unscaled measurements the adjusted Rand index is 0.7302 and the best-match agreement is 134 of 150, or 89.33 per cent.

The structure of the errors is more informative than the total. Setosa is recovered perfectly, all 50 in a cluster of its own with nothing else in it. The entire error is the versicolor and virginica boundary: 14 virginica fall into the versicolor cluster and 2 versicolor into the virginica one. That is not a failure of the algorithm so much as a property of the data, because those two species genuinely overlap in petal and sepal measurements while setosa is separated from both by a clear gap.

Standardising makes the result worse, dropping the index to 0.6201 and agreement to 125 of 150. The reason is that scaling to unit variance inflates the two sepal measurements, which discriminate poorly between versicolor and virginica, up to the same weight as the petal measurements, which discriminate well. Here the raw units already encoded useful information about which attributes mattered, and standardising discarded it.

Task B: Wine data¶

Perform K-means on wine.csv with K = 3 and compare against the three cultivar labels.

The attribute means span from about 0.36 for nonflavanoid phenols to about 747 for proline, a ratio of more than two thousand to one. Proline alone would therefore dominate every distance calculation, and the clustering would effectively be a one-dimensional split on that single attribute. This is exactly the situation standardisation exists for.

In [6]:
wineFeatures = wineFrame.drop(columns=["Wine"])

wineScaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(wineFeatures)

    print(f"  best-match agreement     = {matched}/{len(wineTruth)} = {agreement:.4f}")

Task B results¶

Here the effect of scaling reverses. Unscaled, the adjusted Rand index is 0.3711 with agreement of 125 of 178. Standardised, it rises to 0.8975 with agreement of 172 of 178, or 96.63 per cent.

The unscaled run is close to clustering on proline alone, because that attribute is two to three orders of magnitude larger than most of the others and so accounts for almost all of the squared distance. Once every attribute is placed on a common footing the three cultivars separate almost perfectly.

Read together with Task A, this is the substantive finding of the exercise. Standardisation is a judgement, not a default step. It rescued the wine data and degraded the iris data, and the direction was predictable in each case only by looking at the attribute scales and asking whether the original units carried meaning. Applying it reflexively to both would have produced a materially worse answer on one of them.

Task C: WeatherAUS data¶

Sweep K from 2 to 6 on weatherAUS.csv and visualise the clusters as two-dimensional scatter plots. Unlike A and B there is no ground truth here, so the question changes from how well the clusters match known labels to whether there is any cluster structure at all.

In [7]:
weatherFrame = pdlib.read_csv(f"{datasetRoot}/weather-aus/weatherAUS.csv")

print("Shape:", weatherFrame.shape)
print("*" * 58)
print("Non-numeric columns:", [c for c in weatherFrame.columns if weatherFrame[c].dtype == object])
print("*" * 58)
print("Missing values per attribute:")
print(weatherFrame.isna().sum().sort_values(ascending=False).to_string())

Shape: (145460, 14)
**********************************************************
Non-numeric columns: ['RainToday', 'RainTomorrow']
**********************************************************
Missing values per attribute:
Pressure9am      15065
Pressure3pm      15028
WindGustSpeed    10263
Humidity3pm       4507
Temp3pm           3609
RainTomorrow      3267
Rainfall          3261
RainToday         3261
WindSpeed3pm      3062
Humidity9am       2654
WindSpeed9am      1767
Temp9am           1767
MinTemp           1485
MaxTemp           1261

Two columns, RainToday and RainTomorrow, hold yes/no strings and are removed as non-numeric. Missing values are extensive, with the two pressure readings absent in over fifteen thousand rows each.

Rows with any missing value are dropped rather than imputed. Imputing a mean would place fabricated points at the centre of the cloud, which is precisely where it would distort centroid positions, and with a large majority of rows complete there is no need to take that risk. The cost is that the discarded rows are unlikely to be missing at random, so the retained sample may under-represent whichever stations report least reliably. That is a limitation of the result rather than something the method removes.

In [8]:
weatherNumeric = weatherFrame.select_dtypes(include=[nplib.number]).dropna()
weatherScaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(weatherNumeric)

print(f"Rows retained: {weatherNumeric.shape[0]:,} of {weatherFrame.shape[0]:,} "
      f"({weatherNumeric.shape[0] / weatherFrame.shape[0]:.1%})")
print(f"Attributes used: {weatherNumeric.shape[1]}")
print("*" * 58)

sweepRows = []
for candidateK in range(2, 7):
    fitted = fitClustering(weatherScaled, candidateK)
    silhouetteValue = silhouette_score(
        weatherScaled, fitted.labels_, sample_size=10000, random_state=randomSeed
    )
    sweepRows.append({
        "K": candidateK,
        "Inertia": round(fitted.inertia_),
        "Silhouette": round(silhouetteValue, 4),
    })
    print(f"  K = {candidateK}: inertia = {fitted.inertia_:>12,.0f}   silhouette = {silhouetteValue:.4f}")

sweepTable = pdlib.DataFrame(sweepRows)

Rows retained: 120,381 of 145,460 (82.8%)
Attributes used: 12

  K = 3: inertia =      911,739   silhouette = 0.2294

  K = 4: inertia =      829,797   silhouette = 0.1600

  K = 5: inertia =      764,248   silhouette = 0.1717

  K = 6: inertia =      703,919   silhouette = 0.1677

Visualising the sweep¶

The data has twelve dimensions, so a two-dimensional scatter plot has to project it. Principal components are used for the axes because they retain more of the variance than an arbitrary pair of raw attributes would, which makes the plots a fairer picture of whether the clusters are actually separated.

In [9]:
projector = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=randomSeed)
projected = projector.fit_transform(weatherScaled)
explainedShare = projector.explained_variance_ratio_

print(f"Variance retained by the two components: {explainedShare.sum():.1%} "
      f"({explainedShare[0]:.1%} and {explainedShare[1]:.1%})")

plotSample = nplib.random.default_rng(randomSeed).choice(
    len(projected), size=8000, replace=False
)

figure, axesGrid = pltlib.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16, 9))
axesGrid = axesGrid.ravel()

for position, candidateK in enumerate(range(2, 7)):
    fitted = fitClustering(weatherScaled, candidateK)
    axis = axesGrid[position]
    axis.scatter(
        projected[plotSample, 0], projected[plotSample, 1],
        c=fitted.labels_[plotSample], s=3, alpha=0.35, cmap="viridis",
    )
    centroidsProjected = projector.transform(fitted.cluster_centers_)
    axis.scatter(
        centroidsProjected[:, 0], centroidsProjected[:, 1],
        c="red", s=180, marker="X", edgecolors="black", linewidths=1.2,
    )
    axis.set_title(f"K = {candidateK}")
    axis.set_xlabel("First principal component")
    axis.set_ylabel("Second principal component")

axesGrid[5].plot(sweepTable["K"], sweepTable["Inertia"], marker="o")
axesGrid[5].set_title("Inertia against K")
axesGrid[5].set_xlabel("K")
axesGrid[5].set_ylabel("Inertia")

pltlib.tight_layout()
pltlib.show()

Variance retained by the two components: 60.3% (39.5% and 20.7%)

Task C results¶

Inertia falls monotonically as K rises, from about 1.07 million at K = 2 to about 0.70 million at K = 6, which it must do by construction: more centroids always reduce within-cluster distance. The reduction is largest from K = 2 to K = 3 (around 157,900) and shrinks steadily thereafter, so the elbow, such as it is, sits at K = 3.

The silhouette coefficient tells a less encouraging story. It is highest at K = 2 (0.2375), falls to 0.2294 at K = 3, and drops sharply to 0.1600 at K = 4 before recovering slightly. Every value is low. A silhouette near zero means the average point sits about as close to a neighbouring cluster as to its own, so the partitions are not well separated.

The scatter plots agree with the coefficient rather than with the elbow. The projected data forms one broad continuous cloud, and the cluster boundaries cut through it as clean straight divisions with no visible gaps along them. That appearance is exactly what k-means produces when it is asked to partition continuous data: it will always return K tidy convex regions and report convergence, whether or not any grouping exists.

The honest conclusion is that daily weather observations vary continuously rather than falling into natural types, and the sensible reading of these clusters is as a convenient segmentation, perhaps roughly warm-dry against cool-humid conditions at K = 2, rather than as discovered categories.

Conclusions across the three tasks¶

Preprocessing decisions dominate the outcome. The choice to standardise moved the wine result from an adjusted Rand index of 0.37 to 0.90, and moved the iris result from 0.73 down to 0.62. No parameter of the algorithm itself had anything like that influence. The lesson is that standardisation should follow from inspecting the attribute scales and asking whether the original units are meaningful, not from habit.

A good score requires labels, and the interesting case usually lacks them. Tasks A and B could be assessed directly because the true classes were known, but that is an artificial situation: if the labels existed, clustering would rarely be the tool of choice. Task C is the realistic case, and there the only available evidence is internal validity measures and visual inspection, both of which here point to weak structure.

K-means always answers. Given K it returns K clusters and reports convergence, and nothing in that output signals whether the structure is real. The weather sweep makes that concrete: at every value of K from 2 to 6 the algorithm produced a confident partition of what the plots show to be a single continuous cloud. Deciding whether clusters mean anything remains the analyst's job.

Professional and ethical reflection¶

The learning outcomes attach an ethical dimension to this activity, and the weather task shows where it bites. A cluster label is an assignment made about a record, and once it is stored it tends to be used as though it described a real category. Where the underlying data is continuous, as it is here, the boundary between clusters is an artefact of the chosen K and the scaling decision rather than a property of the world, yet a downstream consumer sees only a discrete label and no indication of how weak the separation was.

Transferred from weather to records about people, that is the mechanism by which an arbitrary modelling choice hardens into a category that affects how someone is treated. The mitigation is not technical sophistication but disclosure: report the silhouette alongside the partition, keep the preprocessing decisions visible, and state plainly when the evidence for genuine grouping is as weak as it is in Task C.
